title: Gross margin is guided from 75% to a 71–72% trough in Q4 FY2027, then 72–73% in FY2028
subtitle: NVIDIA GAAP gross margin by fiscal quarter, % of revenue (Q1 FY2025–Q2 FY2027), with management's guidance range for Q3 FY2027 and outlook for Q4 FY2027 and FY2028
alt: Line chart of NVIDIA's quarterly GAAP gross margin from Q1 FY2025 (78.4%) through the H20-charge quarter Q1 FY2026 (60.5%) back to 75.0% in Q2 FY2027, followed by management guidance: 74% plus or minus 0.5 points for Q3 FY2027, a 71-72% trough in Q4 FY2027 because memory costs run above plan, and 72-73% for FY2028 as price increases take effect. title: NVIDIA's moat is deepest in libraries (4.5/5) and shallowest in CPUs and cloud (2/5); it is narrowing in 6 of 12 layers
subtitle: Repo moat score per stack layer, 1 = commoditised or behind, 5 = no rival close; colour = gap trend over ~12 months; right column = rivals scored 'behind' NVIDIA (of 12, chapter-15 matrix)
alt: Horizontal bar chart of the repo's moat score for each of NVIDIA's twelve stack layers, coloured by gap trend. Libraries (CUDA-X) 4.5, stable; memory and supply 4.0, widening; scale-up NVLink 4.0, systems and racks 4.0 and ecosystem and capital 4.0, all narrowing; CUDA 3.5, narrowing; GPU silicon 3.0 and DPU/SuperNIC 3.0 narrowing; scale-out networking 3.0 and inference software 3.0 stable; CPU 2.0 and orchestration and cloud 2.0 stable. The gap is narrowing in 6 of 12 layers and widening only in supply. Rivals scored behind NVIDIA range from 4 of 12 (GPU silicon, cloud) to 11 of 12 (ecosystem).

title: The GPU (moat 3.0) is NVIDIA's profit engine; its deepest moats, libraries (4.5) and supply (4.0), earn little directly
subtitle: Repo moat score (x) vs how much of the layer's spend NVIDIA books directly as gross profit (y), both 1–5; colour = gap trend over ~12 months
alt: Scatter chart placing NVIDIA's twelve stack layers by moat score (x, 1 to 5) and direct value capture (y, 1 to 5). Top: GPU silicon (moat 3.0, capture 5) is the profit engine; scale-up NVLink and systems (4.0, 4) and scale-out networking (3.0, 4) also earn well. Bottom right: libraries (4.5, 2), CUDA (3.5, 2) and memory and supply (4.0, 1) are deep moats that earn little directly and protect the GPU margin. Bottom left: CPU (2.0, 2) and orchestration and cloud (2.0, 1) are thin on both. Ecosystem and capital sits at 4.0, 3. All scores are repo judgement.

alt: Bar chart of NVIDIA quarterly revenue from Q1FY23 to Q2FY27 with guidance markers: revenue fell to $5.9B in Q3FY23 and then rose to $96.2B; actual revenue landed above the guidance midpoint in every quarter since Q1 FY2024, and the outlook for Q3FY27 is $108B ±2%.

title: 87 of 144 rival-by-layer cells score 'behind' NVIDIA; rivals lead in only 7, three of them in cloud services
subtitle: Chapter-15 verdicts for 12 rivals (AMD, Google TPU, AWS, Microsoft, Meta, Broadcom, Marvell, Intel, Huawei, Qualcomm, Cerebras, Groq) in each NVIDIA stack layer; count of rivals per verdict
alt: Stacked horizontal bar chart counting, for each of NVIDIA's twelve stack layers, how many of 12 rivals score behind, different approach, parity or leads in the chapter-15 matrix. 87 of 144 cells are behind, 43 different, 7 parity and 7 leads. Libraries (10 behind) and ecosystem and capital (11 behind) are the most one-sided layers; GPU silicon (4 behind, 2 parity) and orchestration and cloud (4 behind, 3 leads) are the most contested. Rivals lead in CPUs (AMD), scale-out switching (Broadcom), inference cost (Google TPU, Cerebras) and cloud services (Google, AWS, Microsoft).

title: The thesis in five numbers: 20× rack throughput, 2.3× from software alone, $279B of supply, 15× more stakes, and rivals still gaining
subtitle: One then-vs-now pair per thesis point; each panel has its own units and scale
alt: Five small bar-chart panels, one per thesis point. 1: DeepSeek-R1 tokens per second per GPU at 50 tokens/s per user rise from about 308 on H200 to about 6,261 on a GB300 NVL72 rack, about 20 times. 2: software alone lifted a B200 from about 2,000 to 4,600 tokens/s per GPU between February and May 2025, 2.3 times. 3: supply and capacity commitments rose from $119B to $279B in one quarter. 4: NVIDIA's private equity stakes rose from $3.4B (January 2025) to $51.2B (July 2026), about 15 times. 5: Broadcom's AI revenue rose from about 12% of NVIDIA's data-center revenue (2024-25 average) to about 19% in calendar Q3 2026.

title: Est.: NVFP4 lets a B200 serve ~2.7× its BF16 tokens/s on a 70B model
subtitle: Modelled decode tokens/s per GPU: Llama 3.1 70B, 64 streams × 4,096-token context, 75% of peak HBM bandwidth
alt: Grouped bar chart of modelled decode throughput per GPU for Llama 3.1 70B with 64 concurrent users. H100: about 712 tokens/s at BF16 and 1,424 at FP8 (no FP4). B200: 1,700 at BF16, 3,400 at FP8 and 4,664 at NVFP4. Rubin: 4,080, 8,159 and 11,195. Every case is limited by memory bandwidth, so fewer bytes per weight translate almost directly into more tokens per GPU and per dollar; Rubin at NVFP4 serves about 16 times H100 at BF16. Estimates from a roofline model.

title: Dies hit ~95% of the 858 mm² reticle by Volta; NVIDIA now scales by adding dies
subtitle: Area per compute die, mm², vs the ~858 mm² lithography reticle limit; dies per package and total silicon labeled
alt: Bar chart of die area per NVIDIA GPU compute die against the 858 mm2 reticle limit: P100 610 mm2, V100 815, A100 826 and H100 814 mm2 sit at about 95 percent of the limit; Blackwell and Rubin use two reticle-sized dies (about 1,600 mm2 of compute silicon, estimated) and Rubin Ultra four (about 3,200 mm2), so scaling now comes from packaging more dies rather than larger ones.

title: Rubin's 35 PFLOPS dense FP4 is 280× V100's 16-bit peak; 16-bit alone grew 32×
subtitle: Dense peak PFLOPS per GPU package by number format, Volta → Rubin Ultra (no sparsity; log scale)
alt: Log-scale line chart of dense peak compute per NVIDIA GPU by format from V100 (2017) to Rubin Ultra (2027 roadmap). Rubin reaches 35 PFLOPS FP4 and 17.5 PFLOPS FP8, 280 times V100's 125 TFLOPS FP16, while 16-bit throughput grew only 32 times and FP64 fell to about 1.4 TFLOPS on Blackwell Ultra before recovering to 33 TFLOPS on Rubin.

title: One H100 does ~541K 16-bit FLOPs per clock, ~4× a 128-core AMX Xeon
subtitle: Peak dense matrix FLOPs per clock cycle (BF16/FP16) by compute unit and by whole chip; vendor figures and repo arithmetic
alt: Log-scale horizontal bar chart of peak 16-bit matrix FLOPs per clock. One CPU core without AMX does 64, with AMX 1,024; an NVIDIA V100 SM 1,024, A100 SM 2,048 and H100 SM 4,096; a Google TPU v4 128x128 systolic array 32,768 and an Ironwood 256x256 array 131,072. Whole chips: a 128-core Xeon with AMX about 131,072, a TPU v4 chip 262,144 and an H100 540,672, about 4 times the Xeon. GPUs win by replicating many mid-sized matrix engines, ASICs by building a few very large ones.

title: FP64 peaked at 67 TFLOPS per GPU on Hopper; Blackwell Ultra cut it to ~1.4 TFLOPS
subtitle: Peak FP64 TFLOPS per GPU (Tensor Core where available); Rubin native rate shown, emulated DGEMM excluded
alt: Bar chart of FP64 throughput per NVIDIA GPU: P100 5.3, V100 7.8, A100 19.5 and H100 67 TFLOPS, then B200 37, GB200 40, B300 1.25 and GB300 1.39 TFLOPS, recovering to 33 TFLOPS native on Rubin (NVIDIA quotes 200 TFLOPS via emulation); NVIDIA is trading double precision for AI formats.

title: Rubin leads FP8 per watt (~7.6 TFLOPS/W); Maia 200 is next at ~6.7
subtitle: Dense FP8 TFLOPS per watt of chip/module power vs memory per chip; bubble area = memory bandwidth (TB/s)
alt: Scatter chart of dense FP8 TFLOPS per watt against memory per chip. NVIDIA Rubin reaches about 7.6 TFLOPS/W at a reported 2.3 kW (about 9.7 at 1.8 kW) with 288 GB; Microsoft Maia 200 about 6.7 with 216 GB; AMD's best, MI350X, about 4.6 with 288 GB; B200 4.5, GB300 3.6, MI355X 3.6, H100 2.8 and Gaudi 3 2.0. Google TPU, AWS Trainium, AMD MI455X and Huawei Ascend 950 are not plotted because no chip power is published.

title: Rubin and MI455X reach 17.5–20 PFLOPS FP8 in 2026: 3.5× Maia 200, 18× Ascend 950
subtitle: Flagship dense FP8 PFLOPS per chip by year of volume availability (log scale); hollow = announced/roadmap, dashed = estimate
alt: Log-scale line chart of flagship FP8 compute per chip by year: NVIDIA rises from 2.0 PFLOPS (H100, 2022) to 17.5 (Rubin, 2026) and an estimated ~35 for Rubin Ultra (2027); AMD from 2.6 (MI300X, 2023) to 20 (MI455X, 2026, basis not stated); Google Ironwood 4.6 (2025); AWS Trainium2 1.3, Trainium3 2.5 and an estimated ~7.6 for Trainium4; Microsoft Maia 200 5; Intel Gaudi 3 1.8; Huawei Ascend 950 1, 960 2 and 970 4 PFLOPS by 2028.
source: vendor specs and roadmaps; repo Est. for Rubin Ultra, Trn4

title: H100 registers are ~111× faster than its HBM but hold ~2,400× less data
subtitle: Total capacity vs aggregate bandwidth per GPU at each memory level, H100 SXM, B200 and Rubin (both axes log scale)
alt: Log-log chart of capacity against bandwidth for each GPU memory level. H100: registers about 33 MB at an estimated 371 TB/s, L1/shared memory 33 MB at about 31 TB/s, L2 50 MB at over 5.5 TB/s, HBM3 80 GB at 3.35 TB/s and the 8-GPU NVLink domain 640 GB at 0.9 TB/s per GPU. B200: L2 126 MB at about 21 TB/s, HBM3E 180 GB at 8 TB/s and the NVL72 domain 13.4 TB at 1.8 TB/s. Rubin: HBM4 288 GB at 19.2 TB/s and the NVL72 domain 20.7 TB at 3.0 TB/s. Each step outward gives roughly 100 to 1,000 times more capacity for less bandwidth.
source: NVIDIA, Chips and Cheese, repo Est.

title: Est.: two dies instead of one cut silicon cost per GPU ~62%; eight chiplets ~83%
subtitle: Good logic silicon for one GPU (1,600 mm²), $17K wafer, 0.1 defects/cm², Poisson yield; excludes D2D area, packaging, assembly yield
alt: Bar chart of modelled silicon cost for 1,600 mm2 of GPU logic split into 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 dies on a $17,000 wafer at 0.1 defects per cm2. One 1,600 mm2 die (impossible: the reticle limit is 858 mm2) would yield 20% and cost about $3,119; two 800 mm2 dies like Blackwell or Rubin yield 45% each and cost about $1,182; four 400 mm2 dies about $709; eight 200 mm2 chiplets about $543; sixteen 100 mm2 about $470. Savings flatten while packaging cost, die-to-die power and assembly risk rise with every extra die.

title: Compute/W rose 37× V100→Rubin, but just 2.7× over H100 at like-for-like FP8
subtitle: Dense TFLOPS per watt of package power: bars = best low-precision format (labeled); diamonds = FP8
alt: Bar chart of dense TFLOPS per watt for NVIDIA GPUs. Using each generation's best low-precision format, efficiency rose from 0.42 TFLOPS/W on V100 (FP16) to 2.8 on H100 (FP8) and 15.2 on Rubin (FP4 at ~2,300 W), 37 times overall; at the same FP8 format Rubin delivers 7.6 TFLOPS/W, 2.7 times H100, so most of the gain comes from smaller number formats.

title: Rubin's 2026 revision cut HBM bandwidth 13% and NVLink 17%; MI455X now leads on paper
subtitle: Per-GPU specs: Rubin at CES 2026 launch (hatched, superseded) vs revised pages (Sep–Oct 2026) vs AMD MI455X
alt: Four-panel bar chart. HBM bandwidth per GPU: Rubin launch 22 TB/s, revised 19.2, MI455X 19.6. Scale-up bandwidth: Rubin launch 3.6 TB/s, revised 3.0, MI455X 3.6. HBM capacity: Rubin 288 GB unchanged, MI455X 432 GB. Dense FP8: Rubin 17.5 PFLOPS unchanged, MI455X 20 PFLOPS (AMD did not state dense or sparse). Press reports quote NVIDIA tying the new figures to volume production; the cause is unresolved.
source: NVIDIA product pages and statements; AMD; press coverage of the revision

title: Since H100, 16-bit FLOPS per SM rose 2.4× but low-precision FLOPS per SM 10×
subtitle: Left: streaming multiprocessors (SMs) per GPU package. Right: dense peak TFLOPS per SM by format (log scale)
alt: Two-panel chart. SMs per GPU: V100 80, A100 108, H100 132, B200 148, Blackwell Ultra 160 and Rubin 224. Dense TFLOPS per SM: 16-bit rose from 1.6 on V100 to 7.5 on H100, then only to 17.9 on Rubin; FP8 per SM went from 15 on H100 to 78 on Rubin and FP4 per SM from 61 on B200 to 156 on Rubin, so most new tensor-core silicon serves narrow formats.
source: NVIDIA whitepapers and blogs, Chips and Cheese; repo arithmetic

title: Power per GPU rose ~7.7× from V100 (300 W) to Rubin (~2,300 W, Max-P)
subtitle: Maximum power per GPU package, watts (superchip rows exclude the CPU share; Rubin is press-reported)
alt: Bar chart of NVIDIA GPU package power: P100 and V100 at 300 W, A100 400 W, H100 and H200 700 W, B200 1,000 W, GB200 1,200 W, B300 1,100 W, GB300 1,400 W and Rubin about 2,300 W in its reported Max-P profile (1,800 W Max-Q), roughly 7.7 times V100.

title: Rubin runs FP4 8.75× and FP8 4.4× faster than BF16; on H100 FP8 was 2×
subtitle: Dense peak throughput in each format divided by the same GPU's dense BF16 throughput (BF16 = 1.0)
alt: Grouped bar chart of throughput relative to BF16. TF32 runs at 0.5x on A100, H100, B200 and GB300. FP8 is 2x BF16 on H100, B200 and GB300 but 4.4x on Rubin. FP6 matches FP8. FP4 is 4x on B200, 6x on Blackwell Ultra (GB300) and 8.75x on Rubin. A100 has no FP8 or FP4. Each new generation spends more tensor-core silicon on narrow formats than on BF16.

title: Transistors per GPU rose 22× from P100 to Rubin (15.3B → 336B), now on two dies
subtitle: Transistors per GPU package, billions; dies per package labeled (flagship datacenter GPU per generation)
alt: Bar chart of transistors per NVIDIA datacenter GPU: P100 15.3B (2016), V100 21.1B, A100 54.2B, H100 80B, B200 208B on two dies and Rubin 336B on two dies, a 22-fold rise; since Blackwell the growth comes from adding a second reticle-sized die.

title: NVIDIA's supply commitments grew 17x since end-2023, vs 4.4x for revenue and ~8x for CoWoS
subtitle: Index, end-2023 = 1: NVIDIA commitments and quarterly revenue (filings); CoWoS year-end capacity (dashed, Est.)
alt: Log-scale index chart from end-2023 = 1. NVIDIA's purchase and supply commitments rose from $16.1B (January 2024) to $279B (July 2026), 17 times; quarterly revenue rose from $22.1B to $96.2B, 4.4 times; estimated TSMC CoWoS capacity rose from about 15k to 115k wafers per month by end-2026, about 8 times. Commitments outgrew physical packaging capacity because they now include multi-year memory and capacity contracts at much higher memory prices.

title: Since V100, compute grew 280× but HBM bandwidth only 21×: the memory wall
subtitle: Per-GPU growth indexed to V100 = 1: dense peak FLOPS (best format, and 16-bit) vs HBM bandwidth (log scale)
alt: Log-scale index chart with V100 = 1: by Rubin, dense compute in the best supported format is 280 times V100 and 16-bit compute 32 times, while HBM bandwidth is only 21 times higher, so each byte of memory bandwidth must feed far more math - the memory wall that makes LLM decode bandwidth-bound.

title: Est.: TSMC CoWoS capacity grew ~8× from 2023 to 2026, and NVIDIA booked ~60% of 2026 wafers
subtitle: Left: year-end CoWoS run-rate, k wafers/month (midpoint of press-reported ranges) · Right: 2026 CoWoS bookings by customer, k wafers
alt: Two-panel chart of estimates. Left: TSMC CoWoS capacity about 15k wafers per month at end-2023, 35k in 2024, 75k in 2025 and about 115k in 2026, roughly 8 times higher. Right: of about 1,000k wafers of 2026 CoWoS demand, NVIDIA about 595k (60%), Broadcom 150k, AMD 105k and others about 150k.
source: TrendForce, Morgan Stanley via trade press, TSMC

title: Reported plans would take CoWoS to ~260k wafers/month by 2028, ~17x end-2023
subtitle: TSMC CoWoS capacity at year end, k wafers/month: midpoint and range of press-reported estimates (all Est.)
alt: Bar chart with ranges of estimated TSMC CoWoS capacity at year end: 2023 about 15k wafers per month (13-15k), 2024 about 35k (32-40k), 2025 about 75k (65-80k), 2026 about 120k (105-130k), 2027 projected 170-200k and 2028 projected about 260k, roughly 17 times end-2023. All figures are analyst or press estimates; TSMC does not disclose CoWoS capacity in wafers.

title: HBM capacity caps the batch: a 70B FP8 model at 32k context fills 288 GB at 35 users
subtitle: Decode ceiling from memory bandwidth, tokens/s per GPU (all users) · Llama 3.1 70B, FP8 weights and KV cache, 32k context
alt: Line chart of the memory-bandwidth ceiling on decode throughput per GPU versus batch size for Llama 3.1 70B at FP8 with 32k-token contexts (about 5.4 GB of KV cache per user). H200 runs out of memory at 10 users (~388 tokens/s), B200 at 17 (~843), B300 at 35 (~1,086) and Rubin at 35 (~2,606 tokens/s). Rubin's 2.4x bandwidth lifts speed but not the batch, and at its limit KV-cache reads are ~73% of bytes moved per step.
source: repo model (Est.) on Primer P2 inputs, ignoring compute and overhead limits

title: HBM bandwidth per GPU rose 26× from P100 to Rubin (0.73 → 19.2 TB/s)
subtitle: Peak memory bandwidth per GPU package, TB/s; Rubin shown at the revised production figure
alt: Bar chart of HBM bandwidth per NVIDIA GPU: P100 0.73 TB/s, V100 0.9, A100 2.0, H100 3.35, H200 4.8, B200 and B300 8, Rubin 19.2 TB/s (cut from a 22 TB/s launch target in late 2026) and Rubin Ultra about 32 TB/s on the 2027 roadmap; a 26-fold rise from P100 to Rubin.

title: HBM per GPU grew 18× from P100 to Rubin (16 → 288 GB); Rubin Ultra targets 1 TB
subtitle: HBM capacity per GPU package, GB (usable capacity as specified; roadmap hatched)
alt: Bar chart of HBM capacity per NVIDIA GPU: P100 16 GB, V100 32, A100 and H100 80, H200 141, B200 180, GB200 186, B300 and Rubin 288 GB, and Rubin Ultra 1,024 GB as announced for 2027 (2026 reports suggest 768 GB); 18 times more from P100 to Rubin.

title: SK hynix held 50–70% of HBM revenue in 2022–25; Samsung, Micron ~21–22% each
subtitle: Share of HBM revenue by supplier, % (TrendForce for 2022–2023; Counterpoint for 2025 quarters) · hatched = estimate
alt: Stacked 100% bar chart of HBM revenue share: 2022 SK hynix 50%, Samsung 40%, Micron 10%; 2023 estimate 53/38/9; Q1 2025 SK hynix about 70%; Q2 2025 SK hynix 62%, Micron 21%, Samsung 17%; Q3 2025 SK hynix 57%, Samsung 22%, Micron 21%.

title: Serving four model scenarios needs 242–745 GB of HBM: 1–3 Rubin GPUs or 4–11 H100s
subtitle: HBM needed for FP8 weights + FP8 KV cache, GB (stacked) vs memory per GPU (dashed lines) · GPU counts assume 90% of HBM is usable
alt: Horizontal stacked bar chart of HBM needed to serve four repo scenarios at FP8: Llama 3.1 70B with 32 users at 32k context 242 GB (70 GB weights, 172 GB KV cache); the same model with 16 users at 128k 414 GB; Llama 3.1 405B with 16 users at 32k 540 GB; DeepSeek-V3 671B with 64 users at 32k 745 GB, where compressed attention keeps the KV cache to 74 GB. Against 80, 141, 192 and 288 GB per GPU that is 1 to 3 Rubin GPUs or 4 to 11 H100s.
source: model configs in Primer P2; repo scenarios

title: Samsung's HBM share nearly doubled to 33% in a year; SK hynix fell from 62% to 50%
subtitle: Share of HBM revenue by supplier, % (Counterpoint Research); hatched bar = forecast for Samsung in Q4 2026
alt: Stacked 100% bar chart of HBM revenue share. Q2 2025: SK hynix 62%, Micron 21%, Samsung 17%. Q3 2025: 57/21/22. Q1 2026: SK hynix 58%, Samsung 21%, Micron 21%. Q2 2026: SK hynix 50%, Samsung 33%, Micron 18%. A hatched bar shows the forecast of about 40% for Samsung in Q4 2026 (KB Securities, echoed by Samsung).

title: Per-stack HBM bandwidth rose 16× from HBM (128 GB/s) to JEDEC HBM4 (2,048 GB/s)
subtitle: Peak GB/s per HBM stack (bars; axis label = pin speed × interface bits) · ◆ = as run in NVIDIA GPUs (GPU GB/s ÷ stacks)
alt: Bar chart of peak bandwidth per HBM stack: HBM 128 GB/s (2013), HBM2 256, HBM2E 460, HBM3 819, HBM3E about 1,280, JEDEC HBM4 2,048 and SK hynix HBM4 at over 10 Gb/s about 2,560 GB/s, a 16-fold rise. Diamonds show NVIDIA's as-shipped rates per stack, from about 183 GB/s on P100 to about 2,400 GB/s on Rubin; HBM4 doubled the interface from 1,024 to 2,048 bits.
source: JEDEC, Micron, Samsung, SK hynix, NVIDIA

title: HBM stack capacity rose 36× in a decade, from 1 GB to 36 GB; HBM4E targets 64 GB
subtitle: Largest stack per generation, GB (axis label = DRAM dies per stack) · hollow ○ = JEDEC maximum · hatched = sampling or roadmap

source: NVIDIA, AMD, Huawei system specs; Intel; TrendForce

source: NVIDIA DALI case study; DGX-2 datasheet

source: NVIDIA DGX/GB200/Vera Rubin specs; AWS Neuron docs

source: NVIDIA DGX datasheets; NVIDIA Grace/Vera; AWS Neuron docs

title: KV-cache reload: 84 ms over PCIe Gen5, 12 ms over NVLink-C2C, ~6 s to recompute
subtitle: Time to restore one 32k-token Llama 3.1 70B conversation (5.4 GB, FP8) to the GPU; peak one-way link rates
alt: Log-scale horizontal bar chart. A 32,768-token Llama 3.1 70B conversation has a 5.4 GB FP8 KV cache. Recomputing it on one H100-class GPU at 50% of dense FP8 peak takes about 6.1 seconds (estimate); copying it back from CPU memory takes about 168 ms over PCIe Gen4 x16, 84 ms over Gen5, 42 ms over Gen6, 24 ms over GB200's shared NVLink-C2C and 12 ms over a full GH200 or Vera Rubin per-GPU C2C share, versus about 1.1 ms to read it from HBM3E.
source: Meta Llama config; NVIDIA, PCI-SIG specs; repo arithmetic

title: Passive copper reach shrinks as lanes speed up: ~5 m at 25 Gb/s, ~1 m at 200 Gb/s
subtitle: Typical maximum length of a passive copper (twinax) link by per-lane signaling rate, metres; varies with wire gauge
alt: Line chart of passive copper reach versus lane rate: about 5 m at 25 Gb/s per lane (NRZ), 3 m at 50 Gb/s, 2 m at 100 Gb/s (IEEE 802.3ck) and about 1 m at 200 Gb/s (IEEE 802.3dj objective), the lane rate NVLink 5 and 6 use. An NVL72 spine averages about 0.6 m per pair (2 miles over 5,184 pairs), which is why the rack, not the row, is the natural copper boundary.

title: MoE all-to-all measured at 153 GB/s over NVLink vs 43–58 GB/s over InfiniBand
subtitle: DeepEP on H800 (NVLink capped ~160 GB/s) + 400G InfiniBand: bandwidth (left), latency for 128 tokens (right)
alt: Two-panel chart of DeepSeek's DeepEP measurements. Left: expert-parallel dispatch bandwidth 153 GB/s at EP8 inside one NVLink node versus 43, 58 and 51 GB/s at EP16, EP32 and EP64 across InfiniBand (combine similar). Right: low-latency kernels for a 128-token decode batch take 77 microseconds to dispatch and 114 to combine at EP8, rising to about 194 and 360 microseconds at EP256. H800 is an export variant with NVLink cut to about 160 GB/s, so the gap on H100 or Blackwell is wider.

title: Est.: a decode step's MoE all-to-all: ~22 ms on HGX H200, ~1.4 ms on GB300 NVL72
subtitle: DeepSeek-V3-class model, 128 tokens per GPU, 64-way expert parallelism, 58 MoE layers; ms per step
alt: Horizontal log-scale bar chart of estimated MoE dispatch-plus-combine time per decode step: HGX H200 about 22 ms (87.5% of expert traffic leaves the 8-GPU NVLink domain over a 400G NIC), HGX B300 about 11 ms, HGX Rubin NVL8 about 5.6 ms, GB300 NVL72 about 1.4 ms and Vera Rubin NVL72 about 0.8 ms, where all 64 expert GPUs sit in one NVLink domain. DeepEP's measured kernels on H800 with 400G InfiniBand take about 28 ms, close to the model. A decode step at DeepSeek's ~20 tokens/s per user lasts ~50 ms.
source: DeepSeek-V3 config and DeepEP (GitHub); NVIDIA specs; repo model

title: Est.: optics for an NVL72 spine would add ~19 kW and ~$0.7M; copper adds ~0 W
subtitle: Optics power and media cost for 72 GPUs × 1.8 TB/s (648 800G links, 1,296 modules); spine price not public
alt: Two-panel chart. Left: power to drive an NVL72 spine of 648 800G links: passive copper about 0 kW beyond the chips' SerDes, co-packaged optics about 5.6 kW, linear pluggables about 11 kW and DSP pluggables about 19 kW, matching NVIDIA's claim of 20 kW saved. Right: media cost per rack about $0.13-0.19M for copper priced like 800G DACs versus $0.65-0.78M for 1,296 DSP optical modules. All estimates.

title: 9× bigger NVLink domain, same GPU: ~3.5× throughput at 49 tok/s/user, ~0.8× at 90

subtitle: Aggregate NVLink bandwidth of one scale-up domain, TB/s bidirectional (GPUs × per-GPU NVLink); labels = GPUs

title: 72 NVLink wire pairs per GPU since Hopper: bandwidth grew 3–4× via faster pairs
subtitle: Differential pairs per GPU (left; links × lanes × directions, repo calc) and Gb/s per pair (right); hatched = roadmap
alt: Two-panel bar chart. Left: NVLink differential pairs per GPU were 64 (NVLink 1), 96 (NVLink 2 and 3) and then 72 for NVLink 4, 5, 6 and 7. Right: Gb/s per pair rose from 20 and 25 (NRZ) to 50, 100 (PAM4, Hopper), 200 (Blackwell) and about 333 on Rubin's revised spec (400 at launch, with each pair carrying traffic both ways), and 400 on Rubin Ultra (reported). alt: Log-log line chart of checkpoint write time against storage bandwidth for four model sizes at 14 bytes per parameter: Llama 3.1 70B (~0.98 TB), Llama 3.1 405B (~5.7 TB), DeepSeek-V3 671B (~9.4 TB) and a 1-trillion-parameter model (14 TB). source: Meta (Llama 3), DeepSeek, ZeRO paper; repo arithmetic

title: Confidential mode cost an H100 6.85% of throughput on an 8B model, ~0% on 70B
subtitle: Performance overhead of running an LLM inside an H100 TEE vs normal mode, %; one published benchmark (2024)

title: Bypassing the CPU lifted a DGX-2's storage-to-GPU ceiling from ~50 GB/s to 100–215 GB/s
subtitle: GB/s into the 16 V100 GPUs of one DGX-2, by data path; NVIDIA measurements (2019–20); hatched = theoretical sum
alt: Horizontal bar chart of storage-to-GPU bandwidth in an NVIDIA DGX-2: the classic path through a CPU bounce buffer in system memory tops out at about 50 GB/s; with GPUDirect Storage, local NVMe drives deliver 53+ GB/s, remote storage via the NICs 100 GB/s or more, RAID cards in eight PCIe slots 112 GB/s, and all sources together a theoretical ~215 GB/s, about 4x the bounce-buffer path. NVIDIA also reported ~3x better CPU utilization. Vendor figures.
source: NVIDIA Technical Blog; Blocks and Files

title: Without GPUDirect, staging NIC data in CPU memory would use 39–150% of its bandwidth
subtitle: Inbound NIC data staged in host DRAM (written, then read = 2×) as % of host CPUs' peak memory bandwidth; one direction
alt: Bar chart (repo arithmetic): if inbound network data had to be staged in CPU memory before reaching the GPUs, each byte would cross host DRAM twice. That would need 100 GB/s of a DGX-1's 154 GB/s (65%), 400 of a DGX A100's 410 GB/s (98%), 800 of a DGX H100's 614 GB/s (130%), 400 of a GB200 tray's 1,024 GB/s (39%), 800 of a GB300 tray's 1,024 (78%), 1,600 of a Vera Rubin tray's 2,400 (67%) and, for a whole AMD Helios rack, 43,200 of its 18 EPYC Venice CPUs' 28,800 GB/s (150%). GPUDirect RDMA removes this traffic by letting the NIC write straight into GPU memory.
source: NVIDIA, AMD system specs; CPU datasheets; repo arithmetic

title: Estimates put the host CPU's 'infrastructure tax' at ~19–33% of its cores

source: NVIDIA DPU power white paper; The Next Platform; arXiv 2511.06558

title: 128K-token 70B context: 1.1 ms from HBM, 0.2 s from BlueField-4 flash, 4.7 s to recompute
subtitle: Time to move a 21.5 GB FP8 KV cache (Llama 3.1 70B, 131,072 tokens) into a Rubin GPU, by tier
alt: Log-scale horizontal bar chart of the time to restore a 21.5 GB KV cache (Llama 3.1 70B, 128K tokens, FP8): G1 HBM4 at 19.2 TB/s about 1.1 ms; G2 Vera LPDDR5X over NVLink-C2C at ~450 GB/s about 47.7 ms; G3.5 BlueField-4 context-memory storage over an 800 Gb/s link about 215 ms; G3 one local PCIe Gen5 x4 SSD about 1.4 s; recomputing the prefill on a Rubin GPU at 50% of dense FP8 peak about 4.7 s (estimate); and a per-GPU share of Meta's 7 TB/s Llama 3 storage cluster about 50 s. title: Ring latency grows with every node: ~11 ms at 2,048 nodes vs ~0.12 ms for a tree
subtitle: Latency term of one all-reduce across N nodes, from NCCL's default tuner constants (no bandwidth term)
alt: Log-log line chart of the latency term of an all-reduce versus number of nodes, built from NCCL's default tuner constants. A ring pays 2(N-1) network hops: about 11 ms at 2,048 nodes with the low-latency LL protocol and 57 ms with the Simple protocol. A tree pays 2 log2(N) hops: about 117 microseconds (LL) and 316 microseconds (Simple). Inside one NVLink domain, NVLink SHARP has a flat ~25 microsecond term. This is why NCCL switches algorithms by message size and scale.

alt: Horizontal bar chart of AI site power. xAI Colossus 1 about 150 MW (repo estimate for 100,000 H100s in 2024, ~300 MW planned at 200,000 GPUs); Stargate Abilene 200+ MW live in Sept 2025 of a 1.2 GW campus; Microsoft Fairwater Wisconsin about 737 MW of IT power (Epoch estimate, 2026); xAI Colossus 2 about 350 MW of cooling seen by satellite in Jan 2026 against a 1 GW claim and a ~2 GW plan; Meta Prometheus 1 GW planned with its first phase complete in Oct 2026; Meta Hyperion up to 5 GW; Stargate UAE 1 GW (first 200 MW in 2026); HUMAIN's NVIDIA build up to 500 MW.
source: company releases, Epoch AI, satellite analysis, repo estimates

title: Frontier training compute rose ~1,600× in five years, roughly 4–5× per year
subtitle: Training compute of notable language models, FLOPs (log scale); hollow = Epoch AI estimate (often ±10× or more)
alt: Log-scale scatter of training compute for notable AI models from GPT-3 (3.1e23 FLOPs, 2020) to Grok 4 (about 5e26 FLOPs, Epoch AI estimate, 2025): roughly 1,600 times more in five years, a fitted frontier trend of about 4.9 times per year, consistent with Epoch AI's 4-5x per year. Llama 3.1 405B used 3.8e25 FLOPs; GPT-5 (about 5e25) used less than GPT-4.5 (about 3.8e26).
source: Epoch AI; Meta, DeepSeek, OpenAI, DeepMind papers

title: A Grok 4-scale run in 90 days needs ~163k H100s, or ~40k Rubin GPUs
subtitle: GPUs needed to finish each training budget in 90 days at 40% BF16 utilization (log scale); hatched = scenario
alt: Grouped log-scale bars of GPUs needed to finish a training run in 90 days at 40% BF16 model FLOPs utilization: a GPT-4-class run (2.1e25 FLOPs, Est.) needs about 6,800 H100s; Llama 3.1 405B (3.8e25) about 12,000 H100s or 5,400 B200s; Grok 4 (5e26, Est.) about 160,000 H100s, 71,000 B200s or 40,000 Rubin GPUs; a 1e27 scenario about 330,000 H100s or 80,000 Rubin GPUs.
source: Epoch AI, Meta; NVIDIA spec pages

title: Training needs ~16 bytes per parameter, 8× BF16 inference, before activations
subtitle: Memory per model parameter by regime and component, bytes (mixed-precision training with the Adam optimizer)
alt: Stacked horizontal bars of bytes per parameter: FP4 inference about 0.56, FP8 inference 1, BF16 inference 2, and mixed-precision training with Adam 16 (2 weights + 2 gradients + 4 FP32 master weights + 4 momentum + 4 variance), 8 times BF16 inference. A 405B model therefore carries about 6.5 TB of training state, about 81 H100s' worth of memory, before activations.
source: ZeRO paper (Microsoft) and NVIDIA NVFP4 documentation

title: Llama 3.1 8B saw ~1,875 training tokens per parameter, 94× the Chinchilla ratio
subtitle: Training tokens per (active) parameter, log scale; Chinchilla's compute-optimal rule of thumb is ~20
alt: Log-scale horizontal bars of training tokens per active parameter: GPT-3 about 1.7, Chinchilla 20, Llama 3.1 405B about 39, Llama 3.1 70B about 214, DeepSeek-V3 about 400 per active parameter and Llama 3.1 8B about 1,875, 94 times the compute-optimal ratio, because smaller over-trained models are cheaper to serve.
source: OpenAI, DeepMind, Meta and DeepSeek papers and model cards

title: Final-run compute bills span ~88×: $5.6M (DeepSeek-V3) to ~$0.5B (Grok 4, Est.)
subtitle: GPU-hours × $2/GPU-hour (DeepSeek's rental assumption), US$ M (log scale); hatched = estimate
alt: Log-scale horizontal bars of rental-equivalent compute cost at $2 per GPU-hour: Llama 3.1 8B about $2.9M (1.46M GPU-hours), DeepSeek-V3 $5.6M (2.788M H800 hours), Llama 3.1 70B $14M, Llama 3.1 405B about $62M (30.84M H100 hours) and Grok 4 about $492M (Epoch AI estimate of 246M H100-hours).
source: Meta model card, DeepSeek-V3 report, Epoch AI

title: One Llama 3.1 70B stream at FP8 decodes at most ~48 tokens/s on H100, ~274 on Rubin
subtitle: Upper bound on single-stream decode = HBM bandwidth ÷ weight bytes read per token, tokens/s per GPU (batch 1, KV reads ignored)
alt: Grouped bar chart of the bandwidth ceiling on decode speed for one Llama 3.1 70B stream per GPU: at FP8 weights about 48 tokens/s on H100 (3.35 TB/s), 69 on H200 (4.8 TB/s), 114 on B200 and B300 (8 TB/s) and 274 on Rubin (19.2 TB/s); BF16 halves these and FP4 roughly doubles them. Hatched bars mark cases where the weights alone exceed 90% of the GPU's memory.
source: NVIDIA specs; Meta Llama 3.1 config; repo calculation

title: At 128k tokens, one Llama 3.1 70B chat needs ~43 GB of KV cache
subtitle: KV-cache memory for one sequence vs context length, GB at BF16 (log-log); dotted lines = HBM per GPU (H100 = 80 GB)
alt: Log-log line chart of KV-cache size per sequence versus context length at BF16. At 131,072 tokens: Llama 3.1 8B about 17 GB, Llama 3.1 70B about 43 GB (more than half of an 80 GB H100), Llama 3.1 405B about 68 GB, the same 70B model without grouped-query attention about 344 GB (more than a 288 GB B300 or Rubin GPU), and DeepSeek-V3 with multi-head latent attention about 9 GB.
source: Meta/DeepSeek configs; GQA, DeepSeek-V2 papers; NVIDIA

title: Reasoning multiplies generated tokens ~21×; an agentic task uses ~1,100× in total (Est.)
subtitle: Illustrative tokens per task (Est.), log scale: context read (prefill) vs tokens generated (decode, incl. hidden reasoning)
alt: Illustrative log-scale bars of tokens per task: a chat reply reads about 600 tokens and generates 400; a reasoning answer generates about 8,400 (mostly hidden thinking), 21 times more; a 30-turn agentic coding task re-reads about 1.05 million context tokens and generates about 45 thousand, roughly 1,095 times the chat total.

title: At 100 tokens/s per user, B200 serves ~4× and Rubin ~10× H100's tokens per GPU (Est.)
subtitle: Est. roofline model: Llama 3.1 70B on one 8-GPU node, FP8 KV cache, 4k-token average context; each point = a batch size
alt: Modeled Pareto curves of throughput per GPU versus speed per user for Llama 3.1 70B on 8-GPU nodes: bigger batches raise tokens per GPU but slow each user. At 100 tokens/s per user the model gives about 1,273 tokens/s per GPU for H100 at FP8, 2,293 for H200, 4,953 for B200 at FP8, 5,333 for B200 at FP4 and 13,297 for Rubin at FP8; at 50 tokens/s per user the B200 lead over H100 shrinks to about 2.8 times. Estimates from a simple roofline model, not benchmarks.
source: repo roofline model; NVIDIA specs; Llama 3.1 config

title: Google's monthly tokens rose ~134× in 18 months, to over 1.3 quadrillion
subtitle: Tokens processed per month, trillions (log scale), as disclosed by companies; hollow = derived from a stated rate
alt: Log-scale chart of disclosed AI token volumes: Google rose from 9.7 trillion tokens per month (April 2024) to 480 trillion (April 2025), about 980 trillion (mid-2025) and over 1.3 quadrillion (October 2025), about 134 times in 18 months. Microsoft processed over 100 trillion tokens in Jan-Mar 2025 (5 times a year earlier) with 50 trillion in March alone; OpenAI's API ran about 6 billion tokens per minute in October 2025, roughly 259 trillion per month.
source: Alphabet, Microsoft and OpenAI executive remarks

title: Compute binds training and prefill; memory and interconnect bind decode and MoE
subtitle: Which bottleneck binds, by AI workload (repo analysis; Binding = sets the speed limit, Significant, Minor)
alt: Heatmap of seven AI workloads against six bottlenecks. Dense pre-training: compute and power binding. MoE pre-training: scale-up and scale-out interconnect and power binding. Prefill: compute binding. Small-batch decode: memory bandwidth binding. Large-batch decode: memory capacity binding. Long-context reasoning: memory bandwidth, memory capacity and scale-up interconnect binding. MoE serving: memory bandwidth and scale-up binding.
source: repo analysis drawing on Llama 3, DeepSeek-V3, Pope et al., IEA

title: Datacenter electricity could double globally by 2030 and up to triple in the US by 2028
subtitle: Annual datacenter electricity use, TWh; solid = estimate of actual, hatched = forecast range (low to high)
alt: Two bar panels. Global (IEA): about 415 TWh in 2024, about 1.5% of world electricity, rising to about 945 TWh by 2030 in the base case. United States: 76 TWh in 2018 and 176 TWh in 2023 (4.4% of US electricity, LBNL), with LBNL projecting 325 to 580 TWh by 2028 (6.7% to 12%) and EPRI 196 to 404 TWh by 2030 (4.6% to 9.1%).
source: IEA Energy and AI (2025); LBNL (2024); EPRI (2024)

title: One NVIDIA scale-up domain draws ~600 kW by 2027, vs 10.2 kW for an 8-GPU DGX H100
subtitle: kW per system (left) and per GPU package incl. CPUs and switches (right); hatched = not yet shipping
alt: Two bar panels from the shared system specs data. Power per system: DGX A100 about 6.5 kW, DGX H100 10.2 kW and DGX B200 about 14.3 kW (8 GPUs each); GB200 NVL72 about 120 kW, GB300 NVL72 about 132 kW, Vera Rubin NVL72 about 230 kW (reported Max-P) and the Rubin Ultra Kyber rack about 600 kW (144 packages, roadmap). Per GPU package, power rises from about 0.8 kW (DGX A100) and 1.3 kW (DGX H100) to about 3.2 kW (Vera Rubin) and 4.2 kW (Kyber).
source: NVIDIA datasheets, SemiAnalysis and press reports via system_specs.csv

title: Batch-1 decode sits ~200-300x left of the ridge point and uses under 1% of peak FLOPS
subtitle: Roofline: attainable dense BF16 TFLOPS per GPU vs arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte read from HBM), log-log
alt: Log-log roofline chart in dense BF16. H100: 989 TFLOPS and 3.35 TB/s, ridge point about 295 FLOPs per byte; B200: 2,250 TFLOPS and 8 TB/s, ridge point about 281 FLOPs per byte; Rubin: 4,000 TFLOPS and 19.2 TB/s, ridge point about 208 FLOPs per byte. Batch-1 decode (about 1 FLOP per byte) sits far left on the bandwidth slope; batch 64 (63) and batch 256 (241) move right; prefill (about 1,365) and training matrix multiplies (about 3,277) sit on the flat compute roof.
source: NVIDIA and Lenovo spec sheets; repo arithmetic

title: Decode runs up to ~300x below the ridge point; only prefill and training clear it
subtitle: Arithmetic intensity of common LLM operations (FLOPs per byte, BF16, 70B-class layer), vs GPU ridge points
alt: Horizontal bar chart on a log scale of arithmetic intensity: batch-1 decode about 1 FLOP per byte, decode attention and MoE expert matrix multiplies about 8, batch-64 decode 63, batch-256 decode 241, a 2,048-token prefill 1,365 and a training matrix multiply 3,277. The BF16 ridge points of H100, B200 and Rubin fall between 208 and 295 FLOPs per byte and the FP8 ridge points between 563 and 911, so only prefill and training clear them.
source: Pope et al.; kipply; DeepSeek-V3 report; NVIDIA specs; repo arithmetic

title: A 70B gradient sync takes ~5.5 s over 400G InfiniBand but ~0.3 s over NVLink 5
subtitle: Ideal ring all-reduce of 140 GB of BF16 gradients across 64 GPUs (276 GB sent per GPU), by per-GPU link; seconds
alt: Horizontal bar chart of ideal ring all-reduce time for 140 GB of BF16 gradients (a 70-billion-parameter model) across 64 GPUs, about 276 GB sent per GPU: InfiniBand NDR 400 Gb/s about 5.5 s, PCIe Gen5 x16 about 4.3 s, InfiniBand XDR 800 Gb/s about 2.8 s, NVLink 4 about 0.61 s, NVLink 5 about 0.31 s and NVLink 6 about 0.18 s, roughly 18 times faster on NVLink 5 than on 400G InfiniBand. A 1.6 Tb/s Rubin-generation NIC takes about 1.4 s.
source: NVLink, InfiniBand, Ethernet and PCIe specs via interconnect_specs.csv; ring formula

title: TP moves ~17x more data per GPU per step than DP, which is why it stays on NVLink
subtitle: Est. GB sent per GPU per training step: 70B dense model, TP8 x PP4 x DP64 on 2,048 GPUs, 4M-token batch, BF16
alt: Horizontal bar chart of estimated data sent per GPU per training step for a 70-billion-parameter model split 8-way tensor, 4-way pipeline and 64-way data parallel: tensor parallelism about 150 GB, data-parallel gradient all-reduce about 8.6 GB, fully sharded data parallelism about 12.9 GB and pipeline sends about 2.1 GB; for contrast, plain data parallelism with a full model copy per GPU would send about 276 GB.
source: Megatron-LM, ZeRO and ring all-reduce formulas; repo arithmetic

title: Frontier GPU runs keep tensor parallelism at 8 or less: one NVLink server
subtitle: Published parallelism degrees; bar length = log2(GPUs), each segment = log2(degree); GPUs = TP x CP x PP x DP
alt: Stacked horizontal bars showing how published training runs factor their GPU counts: Megatron 1T on 3,072 A100s (TP 8, PP 64, DP 6); MT-NLG 530B on 4,480 A100s (TP 8, PP 35, DP 16); BLOOM 176B on 384 A100s (TP 4, PP 12, DP 8); PaLM 540B on 6,144 TPU v4 chips (12-way model, 512-way data); Nemotron-4 340B on 6,144 H100s (TP 8, PP 12, DP 64); Llama 3 405B on 16,384 H100s (TP 8, PP 16, DP 128, and TP 8, CP 16, PP 16, DP 8 for long context); DeepSeek-V3 on 2,048 H800s (no TP, PP 16, DP 128 with 64-way expert parallelism).

title: A 16-stage pipeline idles ~48% of the time with 16 micro-batches and ~10% with 128
subtitle: Pipeline bubble: share of step time each GPU sits idle vs micro-batches per step, (p-1)/(v*m+p-1)
alt: Line chart of pipeline bubble fraction against micro-batches per step (log scale). With 4 stages the idle share falls from 75% at 1 micro-batch to about 9% at 32; with 8 stages it is about 30% at 16 micro-batches; with 16 stages it is about 48% at 16 micro-batches and about 10% at 128; an interleaved schedule with 4 virtual chunks cuts the 16-stage bubble at 16 micro-batches to about 19%.

title: PFLOPS got ~50× cheaper since 2017 at low precision, but BF16 stalled after GB200
subtitle: System price ÷ dense peak PFLOPS, US$ K per PFLOPS (log scale); low precision = each system's smallest float format
alt: Log-scale chart of system price per dense PFLOPS: about $155K for a DGX-1 with V100 (FP16, 2017) falling to about $3.1K for a Vera Rubin NVL72 at NVFP4 (2026), roughly 50 times lower; at BF16 the best value is about $17K for GB200 NVL72 while Vera Rubin NVL72 is about $27K because its gains and its memory cost are concentrated elsewhere.
source: NVIDIA, HSBC, Morgan Stanley, resellers via repo registry

title: An 8× bigger die costs ~21× more: ~$29 for 100 mm² vs ~$609 for 814 mm²
subtitle: Modelled silicon cost per defect-free die, $17K 4N-class wafer, 0.1 defects/cm², US$ (excl. test, packaging, harvesting)
alt: Bar chart of modelled cost per good die on a $17,000 wafer: about $29 for a 100 mm2 die (579 good dies per wafer) rising to about $609 for an 814 mm2 die (28 good dies), roughly 21 times more for eight times the area.
source: repo model; wafer price assumption from Epoch AI

title: Est. ~$6.4K to build a B200 vs a ~$30–40K price; HBM is the biggest cost
subtitle: Est. unit manufacturing cost and implied gross profit per B200 GPU package, US$ (price = midpoint of CEO's range; hatched = Est.)
alt: Waterfall chart of an estimated B200 cost build-up: logic dies about $850, HBM3E about $2,880, CoWoS-L packaging about $1,100, packaging yield loss about $1,000 and other about $570, totalling about $6,400, against a selling price of about $35,000, implying a chip-level gross margin near 82%.
source: Epoch AI, Silicon Analysts, CNBC via Tom's Hardware

title: HBM rose from ~14% of an A100's build cost to ~45% of a B200's
subtitle: Estimated HBM share of unit manufacturing cost (left) and of all AI-accelerator component spend (right), %
alt: Two bar panels: HBM share of unit cost rose from about 14% for the A100 to about 33% for the H100 and about 45% for the B200; across all AI accelerators memory's share of component spend rose from 52% in Q1 2024 to 63% in Q4 2025.

title: TSMC's capex rose ~3.6× from $14.9B (2019) to a guided ~$54B (2026)
subtitle: TSMC capital expenditure by calendar year, US$ billions (2026 hatched = midpoint of $52–56B guidance, whisker = range)
alt: Bar chart of TSMC capital expenditure: $14.9B in 2019, a then-record $36.3B in 2022, $40.9B in 2025 and guidance of $52-56B for 2026 (midpoint $54B), about 3.6 times 2019; one report says 2026 guidance was raised to $60-64B.
source: TSMC via AP, TrendForce, SemiWiki, TickerLeague

title: A leading-edge wafer costs ~3× more at N2 (~$30K) than at N7 (~$9.4K)
subtitle: Est. price per 300 mm TSMC wafer, US$ (bar = median of published estimates; dots = individual estimates; hatched = rumor)
alt: Bar chart of estimated TSMC wafer prices by node: N7 about $9,400, N5/N4 about $17,000, N3 about $20,000, N2 about $30,000 and a rumored $45,000 for A16, so a wafer costs roughly 3 times more at N2 than at N7.
source: CSET, Tom's Hardware, TechNode, Epoch AI, others

title: An 814 mm² GPU die yields ~44% vs ~90% for a 100 mm² phone chip
subtitle: Modelled share of defect-free dies vs die area; central case D0 = 0.1 defects/cm² (Poisson and Murphy models; no harvesting)
alt: Line chart of modelled die yield versus die area: at 0.1 defects per square centimetre yield falls from about 90% for a 100 mm2 die to about 44% for an 814 mm2 H100-class die; at 0.2 defects it is about 20%; the reticle limit of 858 mm2 caps die size.
source: repo yield model; parameters from CSET, SemiEngineering, Epoch AI
